biography.text: Ibn al-Haytham was an eleventh-century scholar whose Kitāb al-Manāẓir (Optics) treats light, vision, perception, and optical errors across seven books. A. I. Sabra's translation and introduction describes the life accounts as late and sometimes conflicting and surveys the Arabic manuscript tradition. The familiar stories about a Nile engineering project and confinement are not needed for the investigation here and should not be repeated without checking their biographical witnesses.
gaps: Compare Ibn al-Qifṭī and Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa biographies and record exact primary locators.
Collate the Arabic edition and at least one manuscript witness for the passage below.

timeline.text: The Optics was composed in Arabic in the first half of the eleventh century according to Sabra's introduction; the seven-book work circulated in Arabic manuscript form and later in Latin translation. This entry gives no exact composition year. Sabra identifies a 1983 Arabic text of Books I–III as the basis for his 1989 English translation.
gaps: Establish composition and copying dates from colophons and manuscript comparison.
Map the Latin translation's witnesses, date, and translator attribution from primary catalogues.

fields.text: This batch studies one optical argument in Book I, chapter 3: light from the illuminated atmosphere is directed through aligned apertures into a dark chamber, and the observed illuminated spots are tested by screening apertures and interrupting their paths with an opaque body. Sabra's translation reports that Ibn al-Haytham uses the arrangement to argue for rectilinear propagation. The dossier records the historical claim in its own conceptual setting and does not equate it with all of modern geometrical optics.
gaps: Inspect the Arabic page image and diagram/layout in the 1983 edition and compare the cited Arabic witnesses listed by Sabra.
Check whether this passage's terminology and argument differ across the Arabic and Latin traditions.

legacy.text: Sabra's introduction describes the later Latin *Perspectiva* / *De aspectibus* as influential in medieval European optics and documents a complex transmission history. This dossier does not call Ibn al-Haytham 'the first scientist' and does not claim that modern experimental science began with one person.
gaps: Support influence statements with particular Latin manuscript readings and recipient texts rather than a general lineage alone.

passages.chapterOrSection: Book I, chapter 3, paragraph [37]; experiment described in paragraphs [29]–[36]
passages.explanation: The preceding instructions describe two dark chambers and aligned apertures, observation of separate light spots at dawn, blocking one aperture, and interrupting a ray-path with an opaque body. The passage states the text's inference from that setup; it is not presented here as a modern controlled-laboratory protocol or a proof of every modern account of light.

investigations.title: Testing the paths of dawn light through aligned apertures
investigations.historicalProblem: How does Book I, chapter 3 support the claim that light radiates in straight lines, and what does the text count as evidence for that conclusion?
investigations.historicalContext: The Optics examines visible light and vision through a mathematical and physical account that engages earlier Greek optical theories. This case is limited to the reasoning in Sabra's translation of one chapter; broader claims about Ibn al-Haytham's priority, experimental method, or complete theory require separate textual evidence.
investigations.method: The passage instructs an observer to use nested dark chambers. Dawn light enters through a large opening and then through aligned holes in a common wall; the observer marks the expected straight paths and watches for light spots opposite the holes. Blocking one hole removes its corresponding spot while the other remains. An opaque screen placed along a path intercepts the light and causes the spot to disappear; removing the screen restores it. The text uses these contrasts to argue that the observed light proceeds along rectilinear paths.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: Sabra translates the reported observations as separate spots appearing opposite the apertures, each wider than its opening, with the rest of the chamber dark except for weak light; screening one hole removes the associated spot. Paragraphs [33]–[37] describe moving an opaque object across the interval, the spot appearing on the obstruction, and the inference about straight-line propagation.
investigations.reportedResult: The text concludes that light from illuminated atmosphere reaches opposite places along straight lines. This is the historical author's stated inference in Book I, chapter 3, not a claim that this passage contains the entirety of modern optics.
investigations.whatWasNew: No priority claim is made. The case documents a specific setup, observation, and inference in the transmitted text; establishing its relation to earlier Greek and later Arabic or Latin optical work requires comparative study.
investigations.limitations: The project consulted Sabra's 1989 English translation, not the Arabic manuscript image or the 1983 Arabic page. The physical setup has not been reconstructed or independently replicated, and the dossier does not establish which manuscript readings Sabra adopted for each sentence. The terms and explanation belong to the historical text; do not silently equate them with modern ray optics or call the passage the origin of experimental science.
investigations.laterInfluence: Sabra's introduction surveys a Latin translation known as Perspectiva or De aspectibus and its later reception. This draft does not trace the present passage into a specific Latin manuscript or later author's text.

claims.text: This passage contains an explicit procedure, reported observations, and an inference, but it does not by itself justify calling Ibn al-Haytham the inventor of modern experimental science.
